subQuestions.questionText: Cycles that last 3â€“5 years and are caused by businesses adapting their inventory levels:
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B â€“ Kitchin (2 marks)
Kitchin cycles are short business cycles lasting 3â€“5 years, driven by inventory adjustments by firms.

subQuestions.questionText: A decrease in the value of the currency due to market forces is known as â€¦
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D â€“ depreciation (2 marks)
Depreciation refers to a decrease in the value of a currency caused by market forces (supply and demand) under a floating exchange rate system, as opposed to devaluation which is an official government action.

subQuestions.questionText: Newly established firms that still need protection are called â€¦ industries.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D â€“ infant (2 marks)
Infant industries are newly established industries that need protection from foreign competition until they grow strong enough to compete.

subQuestions.questionText: The continuous movement of factors of production, goods and services among the participants in the economy is called â€¦
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C â€“ real flows (2 marks)
Real flows refer to the continuous movement of factors of production, goods, and services between participants in the circular flow of the economy.

subQuestions.questionText: Service delivery to ensure the daily management of cities and towns is the responsibility of the ... government.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A â€“ local (2 marks)
Local government (municipalities) is responsible for daily service delivery in cities and towns, including water, electricity, refuse removal, and roads.

subQuestions.questionText: A nationwide government intervention to create employment using labour-intensive methods is known as the â€¦
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C â€“ Expanded Public Works Programme (2 marks)
The EPWP is a nationwide government programme that creates short-term work opportunities through labour-intensive methods.

options.D: Joint Initiative on Priority Skills Acquisition.

subQuestions.questionText: Issues related to human well-being over a period of time are monitored by using â€¦ indicators.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B â€“ social (2 marks)
Social indicators monitor human well-being over time, including measures like literacy rates, life expectancy, and healthcare access.

subQuestions.questionText: A track of land that forms a passageway allowing access from one area to another is called a/an â€¦
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A â€“ corridor (2 marks)
A corridor is a track of land forming a passageway that allows access between areas, often used for development purposes such as the Maputo Development Corridor.

subQuestions.questionText: Match: Embargo (Choose a description from COLUMN B that matches the item in COLUMN A. Options: A) when a country engages in foreign trade and produces a given good at a lower input cost than other countries; B) a complete ban imposed on the importing of goods from a particular country; C) measured from peak to peak or trough to trough; D) the proportion of income that households do not consume; E) consumption by one person does not reduce consumption by another person; F) economic goods which do not take a tangible and storable form; G) measured in terms of per capita real gross domestic product; H) levied on properties according to their market value; I) extensive increase in organised economic activity to manufacture, mine, farm and deliver services)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B â€“ a complete ban imposed on the importing of goods from a particular country (1 mark)
An embargo is a government-imposed total ban on trade with a particular country.

subQuestions.questionText: Match: Length of the business cycle
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C â€“ measured from peak to peak or trough to trough (1 mark)
The length of a business cycle is measured from one peak to the next peak, or one trough to the next trough.

subQuestions.questionText: Match: Comparative advantage
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A â€“ when a country engages in foreign trade and produces a given good at a lower input cost than other countries (1 mark)
Comparative advantage refers to a country's ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than its trading partners.

subQuestions.questionText: Match: Marginal propensity to save
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D â€“ the proportion of income that households do not consume (1 mark)
MPS is the fraction of additional income that households save rather than spend on consumption.

subQuestions.questionText: Match: Non-rivalry
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: E â€“ consumption by one person does not reduce the consumption by another person (1 mark)
Non-rivalry is a key characteristic of public goods where one person's use does not reduce availability for others.

subQuestions.questionText: Match: Wealth tax
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: H â€“ levied on properties according to their market value (1 mark)
Wealth tax is imposed on assets/properties based on their market value.

subQuestions.questionText: Match: Industrial development
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: I â€“ extensive increase in organized economic activity to manufacture, mine, farm and deliver services (1 mark)
Industrial development refers to large-scale expansion of organised economic activity across primary, secondary, and tertiary sectors.

subQuestions.questionText: Match: Services
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: F â€“ economic goods which do not take a tangible and storable form (1 mark)
Services are intangible economic goods that cannot be stored, e.g. healthcare or education.

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE term for the following description: The curve that indicates the relationship between the unemployment rate and inflation rate.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Phillips (curve) (1 mark)
The Phillips curve illustrates the inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation.

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE term for the following description: An economy that excludes the foreign sector.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Closed (economy) (1 mark)
A closed economy is one that does not engage in international trade and excludes the foreign sector.

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE term for the following description: A strategy to strengthen the institutional capacity to deliver services that facilitate economic and social development.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Integrated Manufacturing Strategy (1 mark)
This strategy strengthens institutional capacity to deliver services that support economic and social development.

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE term for the following description: A regional development initiative that attracts infrastructure and business investments to neglected areas.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Spatial Development Initiatives (1 mark)
SDIs are regional development initiatives aimed at attracting infrastructure and business investment to underdeveloped/neglected areas.

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE term for the following description: A tariff based on a fixed amount per unit, weight or size that is levied on imported goods.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Specific (tariff) (1 mark)
A specific tariff is a fixed monetary amount imposed per unit, weight, or size of an imported good.

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE term for the following description: A business cycle approach based on forces inside the market system.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Endogenous / Keynesian (1 mark)
The endogenous (Keynesian) approach explains business cycles using forces from within the market system itself.

subQuestions.questionText: Name any TWO examples of a strategic industry.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 1 mark per correct example (2 x 1 = 2 marks). Acceptable answers include:
â€¢ Energy (fuels) â€“ SASOL / Eskom
â€¢ Iron and steel / Iscor

â€¢ Chemicals (fertilizers)
â€¢ Mining
â€¢ Telecommunications

â€¢ Automobile

subQuestions.questionText: How does a progressive income tax system influence income redistribution?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct full-sentence response (1 x 2):
Progressive income tax influences income redistribution by reducing the gap between the rich and the poor (higher earners pay a higher percentage of their income in tax, which is then used to fund services and grants for lower-income groups).
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to the South Africa's National Accounts Aggregates table. Which year does the South African Reserve Bank currently use as the base year? (Refer to the table in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: 2010 / 2015 (1 mark)
The table is presented at constant 2010 prices, which indicates the base year used by SARB.

subQuestions.questionText: Identify the figure used to cater for errors and omissions when calculating the gross domestic product at market prices. (Refer to the table in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: R19 097 m (1 mark)
The residual item of R19 097 million caters for errors and omissions in the GDP calculation.

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly describe the term gross domestic expenditure.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct definition:
Gross domestic expenditure is the total expenditure (spending) on all goods and services produced within the borders of a country within a specific period of time.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: What effect would an increase in imported clothing have on domestic textile manufacturers?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for ONE well-explained effect (or 1+1 for two brief effects). Acceptable points:
â€¢ Domestic textile manufacturers would face more competition that might force them to produce less.
â€¢ They might have fewer customers / less market share / lower sales, reducing profits.
â€¢ They might be forced to be more innovative due to high competition from foreign producers.
â€¢ Quality of their products should improve and they will become more competitive in global markets.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: How does gross capital formation impact the economy positively?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks per well-explained point (2 x 2 = 4 marks). Acceptable points:
â€¢ The increased capital base of the country will increase production capacity.
â€¢ Gross capital formation will contribute to the growth potential of the economy through value-adding processes.
â€¢ Balance of Payments problems will decrease through an increase in export production.
â€¢ Households may benefit from employment opportunities, thus reducing poverty / government will achieve its goal of full employment and collect more tax revenue.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to the extract on Economic Integration. Name the institution that promotes trade liberalisation.
subQuestions.memoText: Correct answer: World Trade Organisation / WTO (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE form of economic integration.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 1 mark for any one of:
â€¢ Customs union
â€¢ Common market
â€¢ Economic union
â€¢ Monetary union
â€¢ Free trade area

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly describe the term free trade.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct definition:
Free trade is when consumers and producers are free to buy and sell goods and services anywhere in the world without restrictions (such as tariffs or quotas).
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Why will import substitution have a negative effect on consumers in the long run?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for ONE well-explained point (or 1+1 for two brief points):
â€¢ Consumers' choice will decrease as they will be limited to domestic products only.
â€¢ Consumers may pay higher prices on domestic products due to less competition.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: How could African countries benefit from a new free trade agreement?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks per well-explained benefit (2 x 2 = 4 marks). Acceptable points:
â€¢ Enjoying lower prices on goods and services.
â€¢ Enjoying free movement and job opportunities across borders.
â€¢ Specialising in the production of goods where they enjoy a comparative advantage.
â€¢ Producing goods in large quantities as a result of specialisation.
â€¢ Producing better quality products due to improved innovation.
â€¢ Improving relationships through mutual gains from the exchange of goods.
â€¢ Improving consumer welfare as a result of more choice of goods and services.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: With the aid of a correctly labelled graph, explain the effects of demand-side policies in stimulating economic activity during a recession.
subQuestions.memoText:
Graph allocation (Max 4 marks):
â€¢ Correct labelling of axes (General price level on Y-axis, Output / Real GDP on X-axis) = 1 mark
â€¢ Increase in price (P to P1) shown = 1 mark
â€¢ Increase in quantity (Q to Q1) shown = 1 mark
â€¢ Increase in AD curve to AD1 (rightward shift) = 1 mark

Explanation (Max 4 marks â€“ 2 marks per fact):
â€¢ Demand-side policies involve expansionary monetary policy, such as a decrease in interest rates that encourages borrowing and increases consumption and investment.
â€¢ Expansionary fiscal policy involves a decrease in tax and an increase in government spending which will increase spending.
â€¢ Both policies will result in a shift of aggregate demand from AD to AD1 while aggregate supply remains at AS.
â€¢ Real GDP will increase from Q to Q1 when aggregate demand increases.
â€¢ The general price level will increase from P to P1.
â€¢ Demand-side policies may be used to stimulate economic growth although inflation may increase.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)
(A maximum of 4 marks will be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples.)

subQuestions.questionText: How could an increase in investments contribute towards a higher national income in the economy?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 8 marks (2 marks per well-explained point). Investments will benefit national income by:
â€¢ Increasing the capital base of the economy, to expand production capacity.
â€¢ Creating more job opportunities and increasing income levels of households, stimulating aggregate demand.
â€¢ Increasing competition when new businesses are established, resulting in increased efficiency in production.
â€¢ Encouraging the introduction of new production technologies resulting in higher productivity.
â€¢ Expanding the tax base for government, leading to higher tax revenue / financing infrastructure development projects.
â€¢ Increasing the competitiveness of local businesses on global markets / stimulating the demand for exports.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)
(A maximum of 2 marks will be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples.)

subQuestions.questionText: Name any TWO examples of industrial development zones in South Africa.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 1 mark per correct example (2 x 1 = 2 marks). Acceptable answers include:

subQuestions.questionText: How can public-private sector partnerships contribute more to regional development?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct full-sentence response:
PPPs stimulate the development of infrastructure in underdeveloped areas (combining public oversight with private sector efficiency and capital).
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to the extract on Sustainable Livelihoods of Township SMMEs. Identify the institution that promotes small businesses.
subQuestions.memoText: Correct answer (any one): Small Enterprise Development Agency / SEDA, OR Small Enterprise Finance Agency / SEFA (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Which economic challenge is addressed by small, medium and micro-enterprises in the economy?
subQuestions.memoText:

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly describe the term employment.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct definition:
Employment is when people between 15 and 65, who are willing and able to work, find jobs and in return receive a wage or salary for services provided.

subQuestions.questionText: How do small, medium and micro-enterprises benefit from the Small Business Support Programme?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for ONE well-explained benefit. Acceptable points:
â€¢ SMMEs receive a tax-free cash grant for investment in industries.

subQuestions.questionText: What are the challenges in implementing broad-based black economic empowerment?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks per well-explained challenge (2 x 2 = 4 marks). BBBEE faces the following challenges:
â€¢ The majority of people do not have finances to buy shares to participate in the ownership/shareholding of companies.

â€¢ Fronting has resulted in many people failing to benefit from the policy.
â€¢ A lack of skills and necessary knowledge led to many black women and youth not being able to occupy top management strategic positions in companies.

subQuestions.memoText: Correct answer: National Industrial Policy Framework / NIPF (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly describe the term innovation.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct definition:
Innovation is the incorporation of new ideas into production processes (to improve efficiency, quality, or develop new products).

subQuestions.questionText: How does industrial development promote entrepreneurship in the economy?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for ONE well-explained point. Industrial development:

(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: What are the challenges faced by the Industrial Policy Action Plan?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks per well-explained challenge (2 x 2 = 4 marks). Acceptable points:
â€¢ A lack of policy coherence and programme alignment.
â€¢ The opening-up of the economy to a diversity of participants has not happened.
â€¢ Concentration and vertical integration within sectors has increased since 1994, reinforced by high barriers to entry.
â€¢ High private sector input costs (steel, chemicals and products in the plastics value-chain) remain a continuing constraint on the competitiveness of SA manufacturing.
â€¢ Continued escalation of electricity costs.
â€¢ High port charges and inefficiencies are a significant barrier and constraint on the export of value-added goods.
â€¢ Current structure of the SA economy is ill suited to the creation of large numbers of jobs at appropriate skill levels.
â€¢ Inadequate state support for investment, upgrading, innovation and technology.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss the general benchmark criteria for regional development.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks per well-explained criterion (4 x 2 = 8 marks). Acceptable points:
â€¢ Good governance: requires democratic decision-making, transparency, financial management and control.
â€¢ Integrated approach: ensures the benefits of one region spill over to other industries and areas.
â€¢ Partnerships: should be built between central government and the private sector.
â€¢ Provision of resources: should be sufficiently provided in poorly resourced areas.
â€¢ Competitiveness: industries and businesses established as a result of regional policies should not need ongoing financial aid from government.
â€¢ Development of people, for people, by people: aims to serve people through training, education, improving productivity and providing essential goods and services to raise standards of living.
â€¢ Development from below: concentrate on issues at grassroots level where most urgent human needs exist; starts by dealing with poverty.
â€¢ Total development as a multi-dimensional process: treat development from a global perspective covering all human life, including the interaction of special forces in a community (e.g. education, health, nutrition).
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)
(A maximum of 4 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples.)

subQuestions.questionText: Evaluate the use of supply-side measures in solving the persistent low economic growth in South Africa.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 8 marks (2 marks per well-explained point). Supply-side measures have been successful in solving low economic growth by:
â€¢ Offering incentives such as cash grants and subsidies to enhance export promotion / attract private sector investments and FDIs.
â€¢ Lowering tax rates to motivate people to work harder to increase income / production levels.
â€¢ Lowering income tax rates may also encourage people to save more / improving availability of loanable funds for investment.
â€¢ Increasing labour productivity through better education, training and healthcare leading to higher production output.
â€¢ Promoting entrepreneurship, establishment of small businesses and new industries to increase competition / limit monopolies and oligopolies.

Supply-side measures still need to be improved in terms of:
â€¢ Ensuring efficient and reliable supply of infrastructure services (transport, energy) to reduce the cost of doing business.
â€¢ Reducing administrative cost (e.g. inspections and unnecessary regulations) by imposing simpler tax and operational regulations.
â€¢ Privatising some state-owned assets to improve efficiency in service delivery.
â€¢ Reducing government intervention by removing unnecessary rules and regulations / ensuring free market operation / improving market efficiency.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)
(A maximum of 2 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples.)

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly discuss extrapolation and amplitude as features in the forecasting of business cycles.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 4 marks for each feature (2 x 4 = 8 marks):

Extrapolation (Max 4):
â€¢ Forecasters use past data (e.g. trends) and, by assuming the trend will continue, make predictions about the future.
â€¢ Something unknown is estimated from facts or information that are known.
â€¢ If it becomes clear that the business cycle has passed through a trough and entered a boom phase, forecasters might predict that the economy will grow in the months that follow.
â€¢ Also used to make economic predictions such as future share prices.

Amplitude (Max 4):
â€¢ The difference between total output between a peak and a trough.
â€¢ Measures the distance of the oscillation of a variable from the trend line.
â€¢ The intensity (height) of the upswing and downswing (contraction and expansion) in economic activity.
â€¢ A large amplitude during an upswing indicates strong underlying forces â€“ which result in longer cycles.
â€¢ The larger the amplitude, the more extreme the changes that may occur.
â€¢ Example: during the upswing inflation may increase from 5% to 10% (a 100% increase).
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Evaluate the impact of the depreciating rand on the South African economy.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 8 marks (2 marks per well-explained point). The candidate should evaluate both positive and negative impacts.

Positive impacts:
â€¢ Exports become relatively cheaper, leading to increased demand for South African goods.
â€¢ Demand for South African exports such as base metals and mineral products will increase.
â€¢ Foreign tourist arrivals will increase because it will be cheaper for them to spend money in South Africa.
â€¢ Improvement in the trade balance as exports will be greater than imports.

Negative impacts:
â€¢ Imported production inputs such as crude oil and vehicle parts become expensive, fuelling cost-push inflation.
â€¢ Higher cost of imported production inputs will decrease domestic production and economic growth.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)
(A maximum of 2 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples.)

subQuestions.questionText:
â€¢ Discuss, in detail, the objectives of the public sector. (26 marks)
â€¢ How will public sector failure negatively influence economic stability in South Africa? (10 marks) [40]
subQuestions.memoText:
ESSAY MARK ALLOCATION:
â€¢ Introduction: Max 2
â€¢ Body â€“ Main part: Max 26
â€¢ Body â€“ Additional part: Max 10
â€¢ Conclusion: Max 2
TOTAL: 40

INTRODUCTION (Max 2):
The government responds to market failure by establishing and maintaining state-owned enterprises to provide public goods and services.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

BODY: MAIN PART (Max 26) â€“ Discuss objectives of the public sector:

1. ECONOMIC GROWTH
â€¢ An increase in the production of goods and services by the economy.
â€¢ Measured in terms of an increase in real GDP.
â€¢ Real GDP is the value of goods produced in the country after the effects of inflation have been taken into account.
â€¢ For economic development to occur, the economic growth rate must be higher than the population growth rate.
â€¢ A high economic growth rate also means fewer people are dependent on the state to satisfy their basic needs.
â€¢ The state tries to ensure continual growth in capacity because it leads to an improvement in the standard of living.

2. FULL EMPLOYMENT
â€¢ Attaining high levels of employment is one of the most important economic objectives.
â€¢ Full employment means all persons who would like to work and who are looking for work should be able to find work or create work for themselves.
â€¢ The unemployment rate increased over the past few years and above 30% after Covid-19.
â€¢ Informal sector activities must be promoted because it is an area where employment increases.
â€¢ In the short-run, the state accelerates employment creation through direct employment schemes, targeted subsidies and expansionary macroeconomic packages.
â€¢ Over the medium term, the state supports labour-intensive activities in the agricultural and light manufacturing sectors.
â€¢ Over the longer run, as full employment is achieved, the state supports knowledge-intensive and capital-intensive sectors to remain competitive.

3. EXCHANGE RATE STABILITY / BALANCE OF PAYMENTS (BoP) EQUILIBRIUM
â€¢ Depreciation and appreciation of a currency create uncertainty for producers and traders and should therefore be limited.
â€¢ Government uses monetary and fiscal policies to ensure the exchange rate remains relatively stable.
â€¢ BoP equilibrium influences the flow of goods, services and capital in a country.
â€¢ Exchange rate stability has a strong impact on the inflation rate and other macroeconomic variables.
â€¢ The choice and management of an exchange rate system forms a critical aspect of economic management to protect competitiveness, macroeconomic stability and growth.
â€¢ More money inflows into a country result in a surplus on the BoP account.
â€¢ The SARB changed the exchange rate from a Managed floating to a Free-floating exchange rate.
â€¢ Promoting domestic production will increase exports.

4. PRICE STABILITY
â€¢ Market economies produce better results in terms of economic growth and employment when prices are relatively stable.
â€¢ In South Africa, relative price stability means that the inflation rate remains within the inflation target of 3â€“6%.
â€¢ Interest rates, based on the repo rate, are the main instrument used to achieve price stability.
â€¢ The benefit of the inflation target is greater transparency in monetary policy.
â€¢ If inflation exceeds the upper limit of the range, the Reserve Bank must consider increasing the interest rate to cool down the heated economy.

5. ECONOMIC EQUITY
â€¢ A redistribution of income and wealth is essential in market economies.
â€¢ There are sections of society that earn a large amount of money while others earn very little.
â€¢ Progressive income tax and tax on profits, wealth and expenditure are used to finance free social services.
â€¢ Basic education, primary healthcare, basic economic services and cash grants to poor and other vulnerable people will enhance economic equity.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

ADDITIONAL PART (Max 10) â€“ Public sector failure impacts negatively on economic stability by:
â€¢ Causing price instability which depresses consumer spending.
â€¢ Causing policy uncertainty which may reduce investors' confidence.
â€¢ Increasing unemployment as the economy fails to create new job opportunities.
â€¢ Discouraging exporters due to exchange rate instability.
â€¢ Reducing the volume of exports which may increase the BoP deficit.
â€¢ Exposing the economy to a recession due to lack of real GDP growth.
â€¢ Increasing the fiscal burden due to wastage of resources especially by parastatals.
â€¢ Decreasing production of goods and services as parastatals/state-owned enterprises fail to supply key input services (e.g. energy and transport).
â€¢ Increasing the cost of doing business in the economy as a result of inefficiencies.
(Accept any other correct relevant higher-order response.)

CONCLUSION (Max 2):
The state plays a significant role in achieving the macroeconomic objectives by guiding the economy through the national budget.
(Accept any other correct relevant higher-order conclusion.)

subQuestions.memoText:
ESSAY MARK ALLOCATION:
â€¢ Introduction: Max 2
â€¢ Body â€“ Main part: Max 26
â€¢ Body â€“ Additional part: Max 10
â€¢ Conclusion: Max 2
TOTAL: 40

INTRODUCTION (Max 2):
Governments use different statistical data to predict economic trends and formulate suitable developmental strategies toward influencing the direction the economy should take. Economic indicators are used to establish the performance of an economy in terms of basic economic objectives.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

BODY: MAIN PART (Max 26) â€“ Discuss economic indicators:

1. PRODUCTION INDICATORS
â€¢ Nominal GDP (at current/market prices): cannot be used reliably because the amount tends to be overestimated due to inflation.
â€¢ Real GDP (at constant prices): the growth performance of an economy is measured in terms of real GDP figures; obtained when the effect of inflation is removed from the data. When nominal growth is 8% and inflation is 3%, real growth is 5%.
â€¢ Per capita real GDP: calculated by dividing real GDP by total population; used to indicate economic development / living standards / compare living standards between countries.

2. PRODUCTIVITY INDICATORS
â€¢ Labour productivity: watched most closely, particularly in relation to real wage increases. In SA productivity increased less than labour remuneration. Measured by dividing real GDP by the number of workers employed.
â€¢ Remuneration per worker: if productivity increases are lower than real wage increases, inflationary pressures will occur. The relationship between productivity and wages is crucial for employers to survive in vigorous markets and workers to survive on their salaries.

3. FOREIGN TRADE INDICATORS
â€¢ The terms of trade: changes serve as an indicator of changes that may spill over into the BoP and may lead to a deficit. Terms of trade will deteriorate if a greater volume of exports must be produced to keep export earnings constant.
â€¢ The exchange rate: changes affect the prices for imports and exports. A depreciation of the rand against the dollar will result in US goods and services becoming more expensive domestically and earnings from exports to the US increasing.

4. THE INFLATION RATE
Inflation: an increase in the general level of prices in an economy that is sustained over a period of time.
SARB aims to keep inflation between 3 and 6%. Instruments to measure inflation:
â€¢ Consumer prices/CPI: weighted average of the prices of a general basket of goods and services likely to be bought by consumers.
â€¢ Production prices/PPI: measures prices of locally produced goods when they leave the factory and imported goods when they enter the country; serves as an indicator to predict consumer inflation.

5. EMPLOYMENT
â€¢ Economically active population (EAP/labour force): persons aged 15â€“65 willing to work; includes formal sector, informal sector, employers, self-employed and unemployed persons.
â€¢ Employment rate: number of employed persons as a percentage of EAP. SA employment rate was 70.9% in 2019 and is not accompanied by similar growth in employment numbers.
â€¢ Unemployment rate: percentage of unemployed persons out of the total number willing and able to work. SA's official unemployment rate was 29.1% in 2019 and is the most important cause of poverty.

6. MONEY SUPPLY
â€¢ Money supply is critical to give early warning of likely changes in inflation.
â€¢ SARB defines money in different categories: M1 (coins and notes); M2 (M1 plus all short- and medium-term deposits); M3 (M2 plus all long-term deposits of domestic private sector with monetary institutions).

7. INTEREST RATES
â€¢ Repo rate: rate at which SARB lends money to commercial banks.
â€¢ Interest rate is based on the repo rate; when the repo rate changes, interest rates also change.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

ADDITIONAL PART (Max 10) â€“ COVID-19 negatively influenced the SA economy by:
â€¢ Shutting down industrial and business sectors, reducing the production of non-essential goods and services.
â€¢ Slowing down economic growth, increasing unemployment / loss of income.
â€¢ Restricting global trade, reducing demand for South African products.
â€¢ Contributing to more BoP problems as exports decreased.
â€¢ Reducing mining and manufacturing productivity due to operational restrictions or scale-down.
â€¢ Restricting movement of people, reducing tourism activities domestically and internationally.
â€¢ Reducing tax revenue for the government due to trade restrictions on non-essential products such as alcohol and tobacco.
â€¢ Decreasing real GDP growth with a possible recession resulting from the negative impact on production of goods and services.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

CONCLUSION (Max 2):
The use of economic indicators is important because analysts use the data to interpret current or future investment possibilities.
(Accept any other correct relevant higher-order conclusion.)
